questions.question: What is the difference between Heap and Stack memory in Java?
questions.title: Heap vs Stack Memory
questions.direct_answer: The JVM heap is shared by all threads and is the logical storage for class instances and arrays. Every JVM thread has a private JVM stack made of frames for its active method calls. A frame carries local variables, an operand stack, and method-execution data; it disappears when that call completes.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Heap: shared runtime area from which class instances and arrays are allocated.
JVM stack: private to one thread and composed of frames for active method calls.
A local variable may contain an object reference; that does not put the object in the frame.
Frames end with their calls, while heap objects remain until they are unreachable and reclaimed.
Deep calls usually lead to `StackOverflowError`; inability to allocate heap storage leads to `OutOfMemoryError`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Heap and stack are different JVM memory areas. The heap is shared by all threads and stores class instances and arrays. Each thread has its own JVM stack, which contains a frame for every active method call.

For example, in `Person person = new Person()`, the local variable `person` is a reference in the current method frame. The `Person` object itself is on the heap. A primitive local value can be in a frame, while a primitive field is part of its object.

Their lifetimes are also different. A frame is removed when its method finishes. A heap object can remain after that method returns if a field, collection, returned reference, or another live path still reaches it.

Deep or endless calls can cause `StackOverflowError`. If the JVM cannot provide enough heap storage, it can throw `OutOfMemoryError`. The simple rule is: stacks hold one thread's active calls, while the heap holds shared objects and arrays.

sections.title: References, Variables, and Heap Objects
sections.content:
**Call stacks and heap objects**

Suppose `createOrder()` constructs an Order, stores the reference in a service field, and returns. The method call has a frame containing its parameters, temporary values, and the local Order reference. That frame ends on return. The Order remains reachable through the service field, so it is not garbage just because the creating method finished.

If the method returns the reference instead, the caller receives a copy of the reference value before the callee frame disappears. If the method neither returns nor stores it, and no other path exists, the Order can become eligible for collection. Eligibility still does not mean immediate collection.

**Memory areas and their common failures**

A recursive traversal creates another frame for every unfinished call. With enough depth, one thread may reach its allowed stack limit and throw `StackOverflowError` even while plenty of heap remains. A program retaining millions of Orders can instead exhaust heap capacity and throw `OutOfMemoryError` even with shallow call stacks. The error points to a runtime area, while logs and traces reveal the actual cause.

**Logical memory areas and runtime optimisations**

If an object's identity never escapes and is unobservable, an optimizing JVM may eliminate the allocation or break it into scalar values. This does not change Java-level behaviour and is not storage an application can request. The JVM specification defines logical areas rather than one universal RAM map, so avoid fixed claims about addresses, default stack sizes, or which allocation is “always faster” without naming a runtime and measurement.

sections.title: Compare ownership, contents, lifetime, and failure
sections.content:
| Question | JVM stack | Heap |
|---|---|---|
| Who owns it? | One thread | Shared by JVM threads |
| Main unit | Frame per active method call | Class instance or array |
| Lifetime | Until the call completes | Until unreachable and later reclaimed |
| Managed by GC? | Frames follow calls | Yes, by the chosen collector |
| Typical exhaustion | `StackOverflowError` | `OutOfMemoryError` |

questions.question: Where are objects stored in Java — heap or stack?
questions.title: Where Are Objects Stored in Java?
questions.direct_answer: Java class instances and arrays are logically allocated from the JVM heap. A local variable can hold a reference in its method frame, and an optimizing JVM may eliminate or decompose an allocation, but Java code cannot depend on a particular physical object address or on “stack allocation.”

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The JVM specification defines the heap as the source of storage for every class instance and array.
A local variable stores a reference value; the referenced object is not part of that local slot.
Fields can hold references to the same object, so an object can outlive its creator method.
Escape analysis may let a JVM remove or decompose an allocation without changing program behaviour.
Object placement and layout are runtime details, not contracts application code should assume.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
At the JVM model level, every class instance and array is allocated from the heap. This includes normal objects, records, exceptions, primitive arrays, reference arrays, and String objects.

The variable that points to an object may live somewhere else. In `Customer customer = new Customer()`, the local frame holds the `customer` reference, while the `Customer` object is on the heap. If that reference is returned or stored in a field, the same object can outlive the method.

Fields belong to their containing object. A primitive field stores its value inside that object, and a reference field stores a link to another object. An array is also an object, so `int[] values` is a reference to a heap array.

An optimizing JVM may use escape analysis to remove a temporary allocation or keep its values in registers. That optimization is invisible and not guaranteed. Java code should use the rule that instances and arrays have heap semantics and should not depend on a physical object location.

sections.title: Variable location and object reachability are separate questions
sections.content:
**Reference variables and their objects**

A variable is a storage location holding a value; an object is a runtime entity with identity and fields. In `User first = new User()`, `first` holds a reference value. Assigning `User second = first` copies that reference, not the User. Both arrows reach one object, so a mutation through `second` is visible through `first`.

Arrays follow the same rule. `int[] numbers` is a reference variable, while the array is an object that contains integer elements. An object field can hold another reference, producing a graph rather than physically nesting one complete object inside another. A shallow copy duplicates the outer object but can keep arrows to the same inner targets.

**Reachability and object lifetime**

Garbage collection does not use the source block where an object was created as its lifetime. A returned reference, static field, instance field, live thread, JNI reference, or other root path can retain the object after the creator returns. Conversely, a JVM can determine that a local is no longer needed before the source method's closing brace.

**Treat optimisation as invisible**

Escape analysis can prove that a temporary object's identity is not observable. A JIT may then remove the allocation or keep scalar values in registers or implementation storage. The program must behave exactly as if normal heap semantics applied. This is why the safe interview model is “instances and arrays come from the heap; references live wherever their variables or fields live,” followed by optimisation only as a boundary note.

sections.title: One object can be reached through different reference locations
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  F[Method frame: local `customer`] --> O[Customer instance]
  S[Service object: field `current`] --> O
  C[Collection element] --> O
  O --> A[Address String instance]
```

questions.question: What is a stack frame in Java?
questions.title: What is a Stack Frame?
questions.direct_answer: A JVM frame is the per-invocation data structure on one thread's JVM stack. It contains local-variable slots, an operand stack, and information needed for dynamic linking, normal return, and exception dispatch. One frame is created for every method invocation and destroyed when that invocation completes.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Every method invocation creates a new frame on the invoking thread's JVM stack.
The local-variable array holds parameters and other method-local values in indexed slots.
The operand stack supplies inputs and receives results for many bytecode instructions.
A frame also carries runtime-constant-pool linkage and return/exception information.
The frame is destroyed on normal return or abrupt completion; recursive calls each need their own frame.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A stack frame is the JVM's working area for one method call. Every time a thread calls a method, the JVM creates a new frame on that thread's stack. A recursive call gets its own frame and its own local values.

A frame mainly contains local-variable slots, an operand stack, and information for linking and returning. Method arguments and local values go into the local slots. Bytecode uses the operand stack to perform calculations.

For example, a call to `sum(20, 22)` places 20 and 22 in local slots. The bytecode loads them onto the operand stack, adds them, and returns 42 to the caller. If the method throws an unhandled exception, the frame is removed while the JVM looks for a handler in an earlier call.

The frame exists only for that invocation. When the method completes, its frame is destroyed. Too many unfinished calls, such as recursion without a working base case, can fill the thread's stack and cause `StackOverflowError`.

sections.title: Local Variables and the Operand Stack
sections.content:
**Values inside one method invocation**

Many JVM bytecodes are stack-oriented. For an integer addition, instructions load values from indexed local slots onto the operand stack, `iadd` removes the top two integers and pushes their sum, and another instruction stores or returns that result. The operand stack is temporary working state inside this invocation; it is not the thread's whole JVM stack.

Object fields remain part of their objects. A local or operand slot can hold an object reference, and field instructions use that reference to read or write the target object. This distinction prevents the common mistake of drawing the complete object inside the frame.

**Connect the frame to its class**

A frame refers to the runtime constant pool for the class of the current method. Symbolic method and field references can be resolved through that structure. The frame does not contain a full private copy of every class constant; it carries the execution link needed by this call.

**Normal and exceptional method completion**

A normal return transfers a result if the method has one and restores the caller as current. An unhandled exception causes abrupt completion and frame unwinding while the JVM searches callers for a handler. In both cases, this invocation's frame ends.

The class file records maximum local and operand requirements, but a JVM chooses its concrete representation. Methods can therefore have different frame costs, and portable Java code should not assume an exact byte count per call.

sections.title: One call moves values between local slots and the operand stack
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Local slot 0: 20] --> L1[iload]
  B[Local slot 1: 22] --> L2[iload]
  L1 --> O[Operand stack: 20, 22]
  L2 --> O
  O --> ADD[iadd]
  ADD --> R[Operand stack: 42]
  R --> RET[ireturn to caller]
```

questions.question: What is StackOverflowError in Java and what causes it?
questions.title: What Causes StackOverflowError?
questions.direct_answer: `StackOverflowError` means a thread's computation requires a larger JVM stack than the runtime permits. The usual cause is infinite or unexpectedly deep recursion, though a very deep call chain or unusually large frames can contribute. Fix the call structure or bound the input before treating stack-size tuning as the solution.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `StackOverflowError` is an `Error` raised when a thread needs more JVM-stack capacity than permitted.
A missing or unreachable recursion base case is the most common cause.
Large valid recursion depth and mutually recursive methods can fail in the same way.
Repeated method names in the stack trace usually reveal the recursive cycle.
Prefer a bounded or iterative design; changing `-Xss` only moves an implementation-specific limit.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`StackOverflowError` means one thread needs more JVM stack space than the runtime allows. Every unfinished method call keeps a frame, so a call chain that grows too far eventually reaches the limit.

The usual cause is recursion with a missing or unreachable base case. Mutual recursion can do the same thing. Even a correct recursive algorithm can fail on very deep input, such as a highly skewed tree with hundreds of thousands of nodes.

For example, `countDown(n)` must move `n` toward the value that stops recursion. Calling `countDown(n + 1)` moves in the wrong direction and keeps creating frames. A graph traversal can also recurse forever when it does not track already visited nodes.

The stack trace normally shows the same method, or a small group of methods, repeated many times. Fix the base case, detect cycles, limit unreasonable depth, or use iteration with an explicit stack. Increasing `-Xss` may help a known bounded workload, but it cannot make endless recursion safe.

sections.title: Depth is a product of algorithm, input, and frame cost
sections.content:
**Recursive progress and the base case**

A recursive method needs a base case and a step that moves every path toward it. `visit(node.left)` and `visit(node.right)` terminate for a true tree because each call moves to a smaller subtree and null is the base case. If the input is actually a graph with a back edge, the same code can revisit a node forever unless it keeps a visited set.

**Repeated stack frames in the trace**

Direct recursion repeats one method name. Mutual recursion repeats a small cycle such as `parseExpression → parseTerm → parseExpression`. The first useful frame in application code often identifies the input and condition that stopped progress. Do not hide the evidence by broadly catching `Error`.

**Structural fixes for excessive recursion**

Correct a missing base case, enforce a nesting limit, detect cycles, or replace recursion with an explicit work stack. The iterative form still uses O(depth) auxiliary storage, but depth becomes data that code can inspect and limit. Increasing `-Xss` may support a known bounded algorithm; it only delays failure for unbounded calls and consumes more memory per platform thread.

Two methods can overflow at different depths because their frames, runtime, platform, and compilation differ. Published universal depth or default-stack numbers are unreliable. Virtual threads change stack representation and mounting but do not make infinite recursion safe.

sections.title: Find whether every call moves toward completion
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  C[Recursive call] --> B{Base case true?}
  B -- Yes --> R[Return and remove frame]
  B -- No --> P{Input moves closer to base case?}
  P -- Yes --> C
  P -- No --> G[Frames keep growing]
  G --> E[StackOverflowError]
```

sections.title: Bounded recursion with visible progress
Audit the termination proof
sections.content: For a recursive tree walk, state the base case, the smaller subproblem, the maximum supported depth, and how cycles are rejected. If one item is missing, the recursion contract is incomplete.

followup_questions: How do you distinguish StackOverflowError from heap exhaustion?

questions.question: Where are instance variables stored in Java — heap or stack?
questions.title: Where Are Instance Variables Stored?
questions.direct_answer: An instance variable is a field that belongs to an object, so its value is stored as part of that object's logical heap state. A primitive field stores its value there; a reference field stores a reference there, while the referenced object is a separate heap object.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Instance fields belong to each object and are part of that object's heap state.
A primitive field contains its primitive value; a reference field contains a reference value.
The object reached through a reference field is a separate object with its own lifetime.
Local variables belong to method frames; static fields belong to class-level state, not each instance.
Exact field offsets and object layout are JVM implementation details.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An instance variable is a non-static field that belongs to an object. Because objects have heap semantics, the field's value is part of the containing object's heap state. Each new object gets its own instance fields.

For `int quantity`, the number is stored as part of the `OrderLine` object. For `Product product`, the field stores a reference to a separate `Product` object. Two order lines can therefore have different quantities but point to the same product.

Instance fields receive default values before constructor code runs: numbers start at zero, `boolean` starts as false, and references start as null. Local variables are different because Java requires them to be assigned before they are read. Static fields are class-level state rather than per-object state.

Changing a reference field changes which object it points to; it does not copy the target object. JVMs choose the exact field offsets, padding, and object layout. The stable rule is that an instance field belongs to its object, while a reference field contains an arrow to another object.

sections.title: Object composition is often a graph, not nested physical boxes
sections.content:
**Instance fields form object state**

When Java creates an object, its instance fields first receive default values: zero for numeric primitives, false for boolean, and null for references. Constructor code then assigns the intended values. Each instance has its own field values, so changing `first.quantity` does not change `second.quantity`. Local variables are different: the compiler requires definite assignment before a local is read.

**Reference fields create a graph**

Source syntax makes `order.customer.address` look like nested boxes, but the useful runtime model is a chain of reference values between separate objects. Two Order objects can point to the same Customer, and several Customer objects can point to one immutable Address. Each target's lifetime depends on every incoming reachable path.

**Copying shows why the distinction matters**

A shallow copy creates a new outer object but can copy its reference values unchanged. Both outer objects then reach the same mutable inner list. A deep copy deliberately creates selected inner objects as well. Neither behaviour follows merely from the word “copy”; the API must define it.

A `final` reference field prevents reassignment after Java's construction rules are satisfied, but it does not freeze the target object. Thread safety and immutability depend on the complete reachable state. Exact headers, padding, compressed references, and field offsets are JVM details; the stable rule is that an instance field belongs to its containing object and a reference field stores an arrow, not the target itself.

sections.title: A field stores a value or an arrow to another object
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  L1[OrderLine A
quantity = 2] --> P[Product
name = Book]
  L2[OrderLine B
quantity = 1] --> P
  F[Method frame
local `line`] --> L1
```

questions.question: Is data on a Java thread's JVM stack automatically thread-safe?
questions.title: Is Stack Memory Thread-Safe?
questions.direct_answer: A JVM stack and its frames belong to one thread, so another thread does not directly execute with those local slots. But a local slot can reference a shared mutable object; the private location of the reference does not make the referenced state thread-safe.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Each JVM thread has a private JVM stack and owns its active frames.
Unshared primitive locals and newly created non-escaping objects need no cross-thread synchronization.
A local reference can point to the same mutable object used by other threads.
Thread safety depends on ownership, safe publication, mutation, and coordination—not the reference variable alone.
Static fields, shared object fields, captured tasks, and returned references can cross the thread boundary.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Each Java thread has its own JVM stack, so its frames and local slots are private to that thread. A primitive local used only inside one call does not need protection from another thread.

However, a local variable can hold a reference to a shared mutable object. The reference slot is private, but the object is not. Two threads can each have a local `counter` reference that points to the same `Counter` instance. An unprotected `counter.value++` can then lose updates.

The useful rule is thread confinement. An object created, used, and discarded by one thread needs no cross-thread coordination. Immutable objects can be shared safely after proper construction. Shared mutable objects need synchronization, locks, atomic classes, concurrent collections, or another clear coordination method.

A local reference can escape through a returned value, a field, a collection, or a lambda submitted to an executor. Stack privacy alone does not make the target thread-safe. Always check whether the object is shared, whether it can change, and how it is published to other threads.

sections.title: Private references do not imply private targets
sections.content:
**Private slot, shared target**

Imagine two keys held in separate rooms that open the same cabinet. The keys are private, but the cabinet is shared. Two thread-private frames can each contain a reference to one Counter object. Updating the Counter is therefore shared-state work even though neither thread can see the other frame.

A statement such as `value++` is a read, calculation, and write rather than one guaranteed atomic action. Without coordination, two threads can read the same old value and both store the same incremented result. A lock or an `AtomicInteger` supplies the required atomicity for that operation; `volatile` visibility alone does not turn a compound increment into one atomic update.

**The handoff also matters**

Safe publication is required even when a producer finishes construction before a consumer starts reading. Thread start/join rules, a volatile write/read pair, a lock, a concurrent collection, final-field guarantees, or another specified synchronization action can establish visibility. Merely assigning a reference into an unsafely shared field is not a complete handoff.

**Check captured and returned references**

A lambda can capture an effectively final local reference and run on an executor. “Effectively final” prevents changing the local variable; it does not make the referenced list immutable. Returning a local object or storing it in a field can escape it in the same way. Ask about ownership, escape, mutation, and publication before calling anything thread-safe.

sections.title: Private frames can still point to one shared object
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Thread A frame
local `counter`] --> S[Shared Counter
mutable value]
  B[Thread B frame
local `counter`] --> S
  S --> R{Coordinated access?}
  R -- No --> D[Possible data race / lost update]
  R -- Yes --> C[Defined visibility and atomicity]
```

sections.title: Each task has a local reference to one atomic object
Test ownership, sharing, and mutation
sections.content: For any local reference, answer three questions: can it escape this thread, can another thread reach the same target, and can that target change? Only the final two together create shared-mutable-state coordination work.

questions.question: What happens to stack memory when a method returns?
questions.title: What Happens to Stack Memory on Method Return?
questions.direct_answer: When a method completes normally or abruptly, its JVM frame is destroyed and the caller's frame becomes current again if one exists. Local slots disappear with the frame, but any object they referenced remains alive while another reachable path still points to it.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A frame ends whether the method returns normally or completes abruptly with an uncaught exception.
A returned value is transferred to the caller before the callee frame is gone.
The callee's local-variable and operand-stack state no longer belongs to an active call.
Referenced objects are not automatically collected; reachability from all live roots decides eligibility.
A `finally` block normally runs before completion, subject to abrupt process termination and other boundaries.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A method call owns one stack frame. When the method returns normally, its result is passed to the caller if needed, the frame is removed, and the caller's frame becomes active again. An unhandled exception also removes the frame while the JVM searches earlier calls for a matching handler.

The completed method's local slots and operand-stack values disappear with the frame. Java code does not free this stack memory manually. This is different from garbage collection, which manages heap objects by reachability.

For example, `makeName()` can create a `StringBuilder`, build a `String`, and return the String reference. The `makeName` frame disappears, but the returned String stays alive while the caller holds it. The builder may become eligible for collection if no reference still reaches it.

A method can also keep an object alive by storing its reference in a field, collection, or static variable. `finally` and try-with-resources cleanup run before normal method completion where their rules apply. The key distinction is simple: a frame follows the method call, while an object's lifetime follows reachability.

sections.title: Return and exception unwinding both remove frames
sections.content:
**Normal return transfers before cleanup of the frame**

A return instruction supplies the caller with a value, if the method has one, and the callee invocation ends. The returned value might be a primitive or a reference. Copying a reference to the caller preserves a path to the same object; it does not move the object from one memory area to another.

**Exceptions unwind a different route**

When an exception has no matching handler in the current method, that invocation completes abruptly. Its frame is removed while the JVM searches a calling frame. Applicable `finally` logic and try-with-resources cleanup run as control leaves their constructs, and cleanup can add a suppressed exception or even replace the completion if it throws. Either normal or abrupt completion ends the frame.

**Object and resource lifetimes need separate rules**

An object becomes eligible for collection only when no live root path reaches it. A method may expose an object through a return value, field, collection, task, or native reference, so return says nothing by itself about object death. Collection timing is then chosen by the runtime.

Files, sockets, database connections, and locks should not depend on either local-variable lifetime or eventual garbage collection. An optimizer may consider a local dead before its source closing brace, and GC is not deterministic resource cleanup. Define ownership explicitly and close resources with try-with-resources or the API's matching release operation.

sections.title: A returned reference crosses the frame boundary
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Caller frame
  participant M as makeName frame
  participant H as Heap String
  C->>M: invoke makeName()
  M->>H: create result
  M-->>C: return reference
  Note over M: callee frame destroyed
  C->>H: use returned String
```

questions.question: What is the String pool and where does it live in JVM memory?
questions.title: What is the String Pool?
questions.direct_answer: The String pool is the JVM's canonical set of interned String values. String literals and string-valued constant expressions are interned, and `String.intern()` returns the pooled representative equal to a String. In HotSpot, pooled String objects are heap objects, but the specification does not promise one physical table layout.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Equal interned strings share one canonical String reference for the life of that pooled entry.
String literals and string-valued constant expressions are interned by language/runtime rules.
`value.intern()` returns a pooled String equal to `value`, possibly `value` itself.
`new String("Java")` deliberately creates another String object before any explicit `intern()` call.
Use `equals` for text equality; never depend on `==` except when deliberately teaching identity.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The String pool stores one canonical reference for each interned text value. Java automatically interns string literals and string-valued constant expressions, so repeated literals can share the same String object.

For example, two uses of the literal `"java"` normally point to the same pooled String. `new String("java")` creates a different object with the same characters, so `equals` returns true but `==` returns false. Calling `intern()` on that new String returns the pooled reference.

Runtime-created text is not automatically the pooled reference just because its characters match a literal. A concatenation involving variables produces a normal String unless the program explicitly interns it. Application code should still use `equals` for text comparison because `==` checks object identity.

The Java API defines the canonical behaviour, not one required table layout or physical address. In current HotSpot, interned String objects live in the managed heap; PermGen explanations describe older JVMs. Interning a small repeated vocabulary can help, but interning unbounded user data is not a safe general-purpose cache.

sections.title: Compile-time and runtime concatenation take different paths
sections.content:
**Automatic string interning**

A literal such as `"java"` is interned. The compiler can also fold the constant expression `"ja" + "va"`, so it denotes the same interned value. If one operand is a runtime variable, concatenation happens during execution and the resulting String is not guaranteed to be the pooled representative even when its characters match the literal.

`new String("java")` deliberately asks for a distinct String object initialized from the literal's value. Its `equals` result matches the literal because their characters match, while `==` observes different references. Calling `intern()` returns the canonical pooled reference. This is a teaching example for identity, not a reason to compare application text with `==`.

**When string interning is appropriate**

Interning can reduce duplicate identities for a small, repeated vocabulary, but enums or domain value objects often express fixed choices more clearly. Interning user IDs, URLs, or other unbounded external values turns input cardinality into pool lookup and memory pressure. Measure a real benefit before adding it as a cache.

**API guarantees and HotSpot implementation details**

The Java API specifies canonical equality behaviour, not a public hash-table design or permanent address. Current HotSpot keeps pooled String objects in the managed heap; older PermGen explanations are historical. Pooling also does not cause immutability—String is immutable whether pooled, newly constructed, or returned by a runtime operation.
